column1: # Korean sayings selected from English Wiktionary contributors via Kaikki; English readings adapted for Paper Almanac.

column2: Words become seeds.
The darkest place is just beneath the lamp.

column1: 콩 심은 데 콩 나고 팥 심은 데 팥 난다
column2: Plant beans and beans grow. Plant red beans and red beans grow.
The empty cart rattles loudest.

column1: 가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다
column2: Kind words sent out bring kind words back.
Even a monkey can fall from a tree.
The years wait for no one.
The riper the rice, the lower it bows.

column1: 발 없는 말이 천 리 간다
column2: Words have no feet, yet travel a thousand li.
After thinking too long, you play a poor move.
A full granary breeds generosity.

column1: 한 마리의 제비가 왔다고 봄이 온 것은 아니다
column2: One swallow does not mean spring has come.
A habit learned at three stays with you at eighty.
Once you draw the blade, at least slice a radish.
With too many boatmen, the boat heads up the mountain.
Sometimes what you don’t know is medicine.

column1: 밤말은 쥐가 듣고 낮말은 새가 듣는다
column2: Mice hear words at night. Birds hear them by day.
The dogs bark and the train rolls on.
A sincere heart can move heaven.
Leave a hoe’s work until later and you’ll need a spade.
Even a monk struggles to shave his own head.
Sometimes it’s wisest to step out of the shower.
Pull the ox horn while it is hot.
At play with immortals, you miss your axe handle rotting away.
Like father, like son.
What the head fails to plan, the body must work for.

column1: 호랑이는 죽어서 가죽을 남기고 사람은 죽어서 이름을 남긴다
column2: A tiger leaves its hide behind. A person leaves a name.
A half-trained geomancer can ruin a household.
The shaman far away always seems more gifted.
In a famine year, even the calendar adds a month.
Young and old alike go where they are loved.
